question.text: How are profits and losses from exchange-traded derivative transactions of a resident Indian ordinary trader (i.e., NOT a Foreign Portfolio Investor / FPI) classified for income tax purposes in India?

answer.text: As non-speculative business income under Section 43(5) of the Income Tax Act, as amended by Finance Act 2005
As speculative income that can only be set off against other speculative gains
As capital gains subject to STCG/LTCG tax rates depending on holding period (which is the position for FPIs, but not for resident ordinary traders)
As income from other sources, taxable at slab rates without any set-off provisions

explanation.text: The Logic: Finance Act 2005 amended Section 43(5) to exclude eligible exchange-traded derivative transactions from the definition of speculative transactions. As a result, for a resident Indian ordinary trader, F&O gains and losses are treated as non-speculative business income; losses can be set off against any non-speculative business income and carried forward for 8 years. NISM Series VIII p.194 and Series I p.216 both confirm this treatment, while separately stating that FPI derivative gains/losses are taxable under the capital gains head. By limiting the stem to resident/non-FPI traders, the non-speculative business income classification is uniquely correct. The Trap: Speculative classification is the pre-2005 position. The capital gains classification is correct only for FPIs (which is exactly why the audit flagged the original stem as ambiguous - it did not exclude FPIs). "Income from other sources" is not the head used by either the workbook or the Act for these transactions. Note: The original stem did not specify the trader's status, so the capital-gains option was also defensible for FPIs per NISM Series VIII p.194 and Series I p.216. The stem has been tightened to expressly cover only resident Indian ordinary (non-FPI) traders, which makes the non-speculative business income classification the uniquely correct answer.
